sections.title: Identification
sections.text: The typical white form of Inocybe geophylla is a small mushroom with a smooth silky white to cream cap, roughly 1–3.5 cm across. It starts conical, later opens while usually retaining a pointed central umbo; radial fibres may split towards the margin in dry weather. The crowded gills are notched or narrowly attached, creamy grey when young and clay brown at maturity. Its slender silky white stem, up to about 6 cm tall, has no ring and may brown with age. The spore print is dull brown. Odour is mild, earthy, mealy or sometimes described as spermatic, so it should not be used alone for identification.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows in woods, parks and tree-lined paths, most often with broadleaf trees and sometimes with conifers. In Britain and Ireland it is found in summer and autumn. A lilac taxon historically treated as I. geophylla var. lilacina is discussed separately in some modern taxonomies; this plate shows the white form.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Small white mushrooms can be difficult to separate by cap colour. Field mushrooms (Agaricus campestris) are generally larger, have a ring and lack the same silky cap; their gills change colour differently. Other small white fibrecaps can resemble I. geophylla. The white form must not be confused with a safe species on appearance alone, and tasting is unsafe.

sections.title: Muscarine poisoning
sections.text: I. geophylla contains muscarine and causes a rapid muscarinic or sweating syndrome. The Belgian Poison Centre gives an onset from a few minutes to two hours, with salivation, sweating, tearing, runny nose, sometimes vomiting, diarrhoea, slow pulse or breathing difficulty. Symptoms often resolve within a day after treatment, but severe respiratory or cardiovascular effects need urgent care; atropine is sometimes used by clinicians. The severity depends on dose and the person affected.

traits: Small silky white to cream conical cap, later flatter with pointed umbo
Crowded notched to narrowly attached gills, creamy grey then clay brown
Thin silky white stem without a ring, sometimes clay-brown with age
Odour mild to earthy or mealy, sometimes spermatic, not a dependable test
Under broadleaf trees and sometimes conifers in summer and autumn
safetyNote: Poisonous: Inocybe geophylla contains muscarine. Sweating, excessive saliva, tears and breathing difficulty may begin within minutes to two hours after ingestion. Do not eat; seek prompt poison-centre or medical advice. Clinicians may use atropine when needed.
